title: Cadi and the Cloud Kitten's Whistle
markdown:
Cadi the corgi was, by all accounts, an utterly sensible dog. Her legs were short. Her tail was a happy stub. Her greatest joy was a good tune — not any old toot, a proper hummable whistle-able tune. She trotted the cobbles without much sound and let out a whistle that sounded like sunshine mixed with a happy sigh. Her world smelled of the baker’s warm bread, the dusty books at the library, and Mrs Higgins’ prize roses, which were flowery in a way that made other flowers feel they had not tried.

One blustery Tuesday the wind played a prank. It did not just rustle leaves. It blew something incredibly fluffy over the rooftops. Poof. It landed in Cadi’s garden, right next to her favourite squeaky toy, a rather lopsided plush squirrel. It was a cloud kitten. Pearly white. Impossibly soft. Like a dandelion puff that had got ideas. Big surprised lavender eyes blinked slowly. Tiny almost invisible paws hovered just above the grass.

Cadi had seen chattering squirrels and grumpy hedgehogs who rolled into spiky balls. She had never seen this.

“Hello there,” she woofed, tilting her head.

The cloud kitten blinked.

She tried a friendly yip. Nothing. Then she remembered her trick. She let out a clear bright whistle, a simple rising and falling note. The kitten gave a tiny jelly-like wobble. Its fluff shimmered. A cold-raindrop shiver ran down Cadi’s spine. She wanted to bark it away like a strange leaf. Her paws felt glued.

A tiny green figure scuttled up her leg, feet tickling.

“Cadi! What is that fluffy anomaly?”

Moss the beetle. His shell gleamed like a dropped emerald, and he always wore the expression of someone marking homework. He peered with his many tiny eyes.

“Remarkable. It reacts only to your whistle. Peculiar resonance. The frequencies must align with its… ethereal composition.”

The town was buzzing for the Annual Big Picnic on Saturday. This year the clouds looked grumpy, the dull heavy grey that promised drizzle and, worse, soggy jam tarts. Nobody wanted soggy jam tarts. The Mayor, whose waistcoat always seemed one button too tight, paced.

“If these clouds don’t clear by noon on Saturday,” he muttered, “the whole picnic is off.”

Cadi looked at the wobbling kitten, then at the grumpy sky. A fizzy idea popped.

“Moss,” she said, stubby tail thump-thumping, “I think our fluffy friend might be the answer.”

Moss nodded sagely. “The Weather Tower coaxed breezes and sunbeams last year. If we get the kitten there, your whistle might tune the sky.”

So the mission began. Cadi packed nothing but her whistle and a sensible dog’s nerve. They passed the bakery, and the warm-bread smell tried to hire her for a different plot. They passed the library, which smelled of dust and staying put. Moss made a tiny map in the air with a claw.

Cadi whistled a clear pure note, and Zephyr — she named him that, because he wafted — floated along. Moss perched on her head like a little green helmet.

“Left a bit. Watch that kite string.”

Zephyr was distractible. Oh, so distractible. A dog barking in the distance. A child laughing. He would jiggle and sway, jelly on a plate, and forget the hill. Cadi’s steady whistle turned into nervous toots.

“Not that way. That’s Mr Grumbles’ prize petunias.”

Zephyr drifted toward the most perfect purple Cadi had ever seen. Mr Grumbles, who detested anything that was not still and green, glared until his face matched the flowers. He had once chased a squirrel with a broom. Cadi did not want the broom version of a cloud kitten.

Then a flock of pigeons came down whoosh-thump, squabbling over a crumb. The air thickened with dusty feather-smell. Zephyr spun, a dizzy blur of white. Cadi’s whistles went oh-dear, oh-dear. Despair arrived with a sandwich-scent. What was the point? Zephyr was impossible. She could go home. She could chase the red plum that had rolled under the bench. She could be a sensible dog again, which had always been her best trick.

She looked at Zephyr, still shimmering, still wobbling. She thought of picnic faces. She thought of Grandma’s song, the one about being brave.

“No,” she barked at herself, firm.

She filled her little lungs with grass and distant flowers. She pictured Grandma’s smile and the blue of proper picnic days, the ones where the tarts stayed crisp and Mrs Higgins’ roses looked smug in a kind way. She puffed her chest, ignored the scattered tarts, and whistled the Grandma tune. Not a toot. A full clear melody that had room in it for a short-legged dog and a creature made of weather. Friendship. Helping. A sunny day that stayed sunny. Warmth spread through her chest. The smell of bread and sweet fruit tried to bribe her. A plum rolled, tempting as a plot hole. She held the tune.

Zephyr stopped wobbling. His lavender eyes focused. He drifted like a pearly boat on a calm sea, straight for the tall gleaming Weather Tower on the highest hill. With a last gentle puff he nudged the highest antenna.

It was as if a giant, slightly embarrassed hand swept the grey aside. A warm breeze went through the park, cut grass and sunshine. The pigeons settled, suddenly polite. Even Mr Grumbles cracked a smile when a sunbeam hit his petunias and made them glow, which was as close as he came to an apology.

Cadi and Moss, windswept and pleased, hurried to the picnic spot. They found a stray jam tart, miraculously unharmed, sitting by a cheerful daisy. Cadi nudged it, then shared a piece with Moss. Scrumptious. Utterly, wonderfully scrumptious.

She let out a little whistle. The Grandma tune, clear now, confident, full of warm light. A good tune, and a brave heart, had turned the sky the right colour. Zephyr hovered above the tarts like a second, friendlier cloud, and did not wobble once.
characters: Cadi (a sensible corgi), Zephyr (a cloud kitten), Moss (a beetle)
